# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–23 (Complete – Updated 165)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of sixth year** (Chapter 23). Rawdon has discovered Rebecca with Steyne, confronted them, visited Pitt to arrange guardianship of little Rawdon, and is now arranging duel with Steyne. Amelia continues evening vigils at Russell Square. Little Rawdon at school.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opens "autumn of sixth year." Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Brompton Square); Queen's Crawley; Fenmere; Quenwick; and others as previously noted.

## The Catastrophic Discovery and Immediate Aftermath (Chapters 22–23)

**Rawdon's Return Home and Confrontation (Chapter 22–23)**: Found drawing-room blazing with light at nine o'clock. Found Steyne bowing to kiss Rebecca's hand; Rebecca sat in brilliant toilette, arms sparkling with bracelets given by Steyne. Rawdon seized Steyne by neckcloth, struck him twice over face with open hand, flung him bleeding to ground. Steyne wore scar to his dying day.

**Jewel and Financial Discovery (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon flung open boxes and wardrobes, found desk Amelia had given Rebecca containing papers, love-letters, trinkets, and pocket-book with bank-notes. **CRITICAL DISCOVERY**: Bank-notes including fresh note for **one thousand pounds from Lord Steyne**—evidence of extensive financial support constituting payment for sexual favors.

**Rebecca's Aftermath (Chapter 23)**: Remained alone for hours, certain "he would never come back. He was gone forever." Experienced suicidal ideation: considered laudanum. French maid (accomplice, in Steyne's pay) persuaded her to rest on bed with kindness. Maid gathered trinkets from floor.

**Rebecca's Revelation of Heritage (Chapter 23)**: Rebecca claimed innocence before God. Rawdon screamed: "You're as innocent as your mother, the ballet-girl, and your husband the bully." **REVELATION**: Rebecca's mother was a ballet-girl; her father (characterized by Rawdon) was a bully.

## Rawdon's Actions and Duel Arrangements (Chapter 23 – Latest)

**Morning Meeting with Pitt (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1362–1367)**: Rawdon arrived at Great Gaunt Street in evening costume worn two days, blood-shot eyed, tumbled clothes. Pitt appeared fresh and neat, initially thought Rawdon intoxicated. Pitt refused financial help: "Even the hundred pounds that Jane took you last night were promised to my lawyer to-morrow morning." 

**Rawdon's Confession and Request (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1364–1365)**: Rawdon spoke in husky voice: "It's the boy. I want you to promise me that you will take charge of him when I'm gone." Rawdon revealed full circumstances: "It was a regular plan between that scoundrel and her. The bailiffs were put upon me; I was taken as I was going out of his house; when I wrote to her for money, she said she was ill in bed and put me off to another day. And when I got home I found her in diamonds and sitting with that villain alone." Pitt instantly guessed Rawdon intended to duel Steyne. Rawdon asked: "I must leave him to you and Jane, Pitt--only it will be a comfort to me if you will promise me to be his friend."

**Financial Settlement (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1366)**: Rawdon drew pocket-book found in Becky's desk: "Here's six hundred--I want you to give the money to Briggs, who lent it to us--and who was kind to the boy--and I've always felt ashamed of having taken the poor old woman's money. And here's some more--I've only kept back a few pounds--which Becky may as well have." Thousand-pound note fell out.

**Challenge to Steyne (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1367)**: Rawdon knocked at Gaunt House, handed card to purple Silenus porter (red and silver waistcoat): "Colonel Crawley would be all day after one o'clock at the Regent Club in St. James's Street--not at home." Proceeded to Knightsbridge Barracks.

**Meeting with Captain Macmurdo (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1368–1375)**: Rawdon reached Knightsbridge on Sunday morning among church bells, school troops, and crowds; might have seen Amelia en route from Brompton to Russell Square but was absorbed in purpose. Found Captain Macmurdo at home in barracks. Macmurdo (veteran officer, Waterloo man, age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, best shots and riders in England, Rawdon's former rival) was in bed recovering from fast supper-party given previous night by Captain Honourable George Cinqbars at house in Brompton Square with ladies of corps de ballet. Room hung with boxing, sporting, dancing pictures from retiring comrades. Macmurdo was reading Bell's Life account of fight between Tutbury Pet and Barking Butcher.

**Macmurdo's Role as Second (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1370)**: When Rawdon told Captain he wanted a friend, Macmurdo knew duty perfectly—had conducted scores of affairs with greatest prudence and skill. Royal Highness the late Commander-in-Chief had greatest regard for Macmurdo. He was common refuge of gentlemen in trouble. Macmurdo noted bets in regiment and clubs regarding fate of Colonel Crawley regarding his wife's character.

**Rawdon's Emotional Revelation (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1371–1372)**: Macmurdo asked: "Is there no way out of it, old boy? Is it only suspicion, you know, or--or what is it? Any letters?" Suggested keeping quiet if possible, remembered hundred particular conversations at mess-table where Mrs. Crawley's reputation had been torn to shreds. Rawdon covered face with hands, overcome with emotion: "You don't know how fond I was of that one...I followed her like a footman. I gave up everything I had to her. I'm a beggar because I would marry her. By Jove, sir, I've pawned my own watch in order to get her anything she fancied; and she--she's been making a purse for herself all the time, and grudged me a hundred pound to get me out of quod." Macmurdo suggested: "She may be innocent, after all...Steyne has been a hundred times alone with her in the house before."

**Evidence of Guilt (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1373)**: Rawdon answered sadly, showed Macmurdo the thousand-pound note: "This is what he gave her, Mac, and she kep it unknown to me; and with this money in the house, she refused to stand by me when I was locked up." Macmurdo acknowledged "the secreting of the money had a very ugly look."

**Letter Composition and Servant's Report (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1374–1375)**: Rawdon dispatched Macmurdo's servant to Curzon Street to collect Colonel's bag of clothes. During man's absence, Rawdon and Macmurdo composed letter using Johnson's Dictionary. Macmurdo was to send it to Lord Steyne on behalf of Colonel Rawdon Crawley, requesting appointment of friend to arrange meeting as circumstances rendered inevitable. Letter begged Steyne to appoint friend with whom Macmurdo might communicate, desired meeting "with as little delay as possible."

**Curzon Street Chaos (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1375)**: Servant returned: "There's a regular shinty in the house, and everything at sixes and sevens. The landlord's come in and took possession. The servants was a drinkin' up in the drawingroom. They said you had gone off with the plate, Colonel...Simpson, the man as was very noisy and drunk indeed, says nothing shall go out of the house until his wages is paid up."

**Rawdon's Paternal Concern (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1375)**: Rawdon mused about son: "He's a regular trump, that boy...I say, Mac, if anything goes wrong--if I drop--I should like you to--to go and see him, you know, and say that I was very fond of him...give him these gold sleeve-buttons: it's all I've got." Covered face with black hands, tears rolled making furrows of white. Macmurdo removed silk night-cap and rubbed eyes.

## Key Relationships and Character States

**Rawdon**: Complete moral regeneration. Transformed from spendthrift to responsible father. Prepared for death; entrusted son to Pitt and Jane; settled debts using Steyne's money; now arranging duel as matter of honor. Emotional depth revealed: profound love for Rebecca now revealed as misplaced; genuine paternal affection for little Rawdon strong and genuine. Has become Macmurdo's client for duel arrangements.

**Rebecca**: Utterly ruined. Exposed as Steyne's paid mistress. Husband gone forever. Curzon Street household in chaos—landlord taken possession, servants drunk, wages unpaid. Facing scandal and destitution. Only French maid accomplice present for comfort. Recovery impossible.

**Steyne**: Exposed as financial corruptor and seducer. Scarred by Rawdon's assault; wore scar to dying day. Has received challenge at Regent Club via purple Silenus porter. Now faces duel with Rawdon.

**Pitt and Lady Jane**: Jane rescued Rawdon from spunging-house; entrusted with little Rawdon's guardianship should Rawdon die. Pitt refuses financial help; all money tied up. Promised hundred pounds to lawyer tomorrow.

**Little Rawdon**: At school; being initiated into Latin Grammar; thrashed by Young Blackball three or four times. Happy and laughing in black gown and breeches. Will receive six hundred pounds (from Steyne's money) through Pitt if Rawdon dies.

**Amelia**: Continued anguish. Sunday morning en route from Brompton to Russell Square (might have encountered Rawdon en route to Knightsbridge). Separated from son; son indifferent to separation. Care-worn, sad, sleeps little, weeps and prays.

**Captain Macmurdo**: Age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, veteran of Waterloo, best shots and riders in England, former rival of Rawdon. "Common refuge of gentlemen in trouble." Conducting Rawdon's duel arrangements. Has greatest regard from Royal Highness late Commander-in-Chief. Conducted scores of affairs with prudence and skill.

**Briggs**: Lent money to Rawdon and Rebecca; kind to little Rawdon. Will receive six hundred pounds from Rawdon.

**Minor characters**: French maid (accomplice); landlord at Curzon Street; Simpson (servant demanding wages); purple Silenus porter; other servants drinking in drawing-room; Captain Honourable George Cinqbars; unnamed people in registry at Fenmere and Quenwick.

**CRITICAL STATE**: Rawdon and Macmurdo have formally initiated duel process with written challenge to Steyne. Steyne has received challenge. Macmurdo awaits Steyne's response via appointed second. Meeting expected "with as little delay as possible." Curzon Street household collapsed; Rebecca abandoned; little Rawdon's future secured with Pitt and Jane if Rawdon falls.
